paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns decisions from an existing dataset. An important concern is that a policy may choose actions outside the data it learned from. Random Network Distillation, or RND, had previously been judged insufficiently discriminative for identifying and penalizing these actions. This paper revisits that diagnosis and identifies a different obstacle.

The authors show that a naive way of conditioning the RND prior makes its anti-exploration penalty effectively impossible for the actor to minimize. In their analysis, the problem is therefore how the policy can optimize against the penalty, rather than whether RND can distinguish unfamiliar actions. They address this obstacle using conditioning based on Feature-wise Linear Modulation, or FiLM.

This change produces a simple, efficient algorithm built on Soft Actor-Critic that does not require an ensemble. On the D4RL benchmark, the method achieves performance comparable to ensemble-based approaches and substantially better than ensemble-free approaches. The results show that the way an uncertainty penalty is connected to policy optimization can determine whether it becomes useful in practice.
icml-2023-anti-exploration-by-random-net.tldr: FiLM conditioning makes RND penalties usable for offline policy optimization, enabling an ensemble-free method with strong D4RL performance.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ across people, so decision-makers often want to estimate effects conditional on observed characteristics. Observational data complicates this task: unobserved factors may influence both treatment and outcomes, biasing causal estimates. The B-Learner addresses this uncertainty by learning bounds on the conditional average treatment effect under specified limits on hidden confounding.

The method combines results on sharp average treatment-effect bounds with a framework for robust learning of conditional treatment effects. It is a meta-learner, meaning its components can use different function estimators, including random forests and neural networks. This flexibility allows the bounding procedure to be paired with different predictive modeling tools.

The authors prove validity, sharpness, efficiency, and a quasi-oracle property relative to the component estimators under conditions more general than those of existing methods. These guarantees remain tied to the assumed limits on confounding. Semi-synthetic comparisons support the theory, while a real-data application illustrates practical use. The contribution is a way to represent causal uncertainty across different populations instead of relying solely on potentially biased point estimates.
icml-2023-b-learner-quasi-oracle-bounds-.tldr: The B-Learner estimates sharp bounds on heterogeneous treatment effects under specified limits on hidden confounding.

paragraphs: Models such as CLIP can classify images using class names without training on labeled examples for the target task. However, a broad class name may give the model little useful information about what an image could contain. CHiLS addresses this problem by enriching the labels themselves when the classes have an underlying semantic hierarchy.

For each target class, the method creates a collection of more specific subclasses. These can come from an existing hierarchy or be generated by querying GPT-3. It then runs ordinary zero-shot CLIP classification using those subclasses as candidate labels. The predicted subclass is mapped back to its parent, producing an answer in the original set of classes.

Across multiple datasets with hierarchical structure, this procedure improves accuracy both when a ground-truth hierarchy is available and when it is not. It requires no additional model training and fits into existing zero-shot workflows. The finding shows that choosing more informative intermediate labels can improve classification while preserving the broad categories the user actually wants.
icml-2023-chils-zero-shot-image-classifi.tldr: CHiLS improves zero-shot image classification by predicting informative subclasses and mapping them back to the requested parent classes.

paragraphs: Neural controlled differential equations describe evolving systems whose behavior depends on measurements arriving after the initial state. They are useful for temporal data but become difficult to scale to long sequences. Existing approaches summarize sequences using log signatures, yet difficulties in inverting these summaries restrict their usefulness for tasks such as reconstruction and generation.

This paper develops a simplification for settings where training sequences can reasonably be assumed to have a fixed length. The authors express regression or classification as an integral transform. By restricting which operators the transform can use, they make it possible to apply an established decomposition algorithm based on non-standard wavelets, substantially simplifying the operator-learning task.

A neural version of this construction produces consistent improvements across a broad collection of use cases considered in earlier work. The paper also presents an application involving coupled differential equations. The approach matters because it connects a structured mathematical representation to practical sequence modeling, with the fixed-length assumption and restricted operator class forming explicit parts of the construction.
icml-2023-controlled-differential-equati.tldr: For fixed-length temporal sequences, a restricted integral-operator formulation enables wavelet decompositions that simplify learning and improve reported performance.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent that starts without prior knowledge must discover both useful goals and how to achieve them. This paper asks whether language models can supply an initial picture of the task. Its abstract world model represents high-level subgoals and transitions between them, giving the agent a starting point for planning and exploration.

The DECKARD agent applies this idea to crafting items in Minecraft. During its Dream phase, a few-shot language model proposes a sequence of subgoals. During its Wake phase, the agent learns a separate policy for each subgoal and checks the proposed world model through experience. Observed behavior can verify the proposal or reveal errors that need correction.

The authors report an order-of-magnitude improvement in sample efficiency over contemporary methods, together with robustness to errors in the language model's proposals. The contribution is the combination of useful prior information and experience-based revision. Language-generated plans guide exploration, while interaction with the environment determines which parts of those plans remain credible.
icml-2023-do-embodied-agents-dream-of-pi.tldr: DECKARD uses language-model proposals for Minecraft subgoals, then verifies and corrects them through experience to improve sample efficiency.

paragraphs: An agent can explore by treating uncertainty as a reason to investigate potentially valuable states. Translating this optimistic principle into deep reinforcement learning is difficult because policies are learned with neural approximators and stochastic updates. This paper introduces a differentiable objective designed to make optimism directly compatible with that learning process.

The objective takes the form of a two-player zero-sum game derived from an epistemic-risk-seeking utility. It assigns value to uncertainty about the environment, encouraging exploration. The authors show that solving the game minimizes an upper bound on regret, with the two players addressing different terms in its decomposition. They also establish efficient-exploration guarantees that accommodate function approximation.

Their model-free algorithm, ERSAC, applies simultaneous stochastic gradient ascent and descent to this game. The paper additionally describes incorporating off-policy replay data and reports a combined statistical-efficiency benefit from replay and the risk-seeking objective. Experiments show substantial improvements on DeepSea, including over other efficient exploration techniques, and improved Atari performance. These results connect an exploration objective grounded in theory with a practical actor-critic learning procedure.
icml-2023-efficient-exploration-via-epis.tldr: ERSAC turns uncertainty-seeking exploration into a differentiable game with theoretical guarantees and reported gains on DeepSea and Atari.

paragraphs: Controlled sequence generation often aims to produce outputs with a desired attribute. This paper studies the harder case where the requested attribute value lies beyond anything seen during training. That goal is relevant to automated design, including efforts to create proteins with better properties than existing examples, because the desired result is outside the training distribution.

The proposed method, Iterative Controlled Extrapolation, or ICE, learns to improve a sequence through local edits. Training uses synthetically generated pairs of sequences that demonstrate a small improvement in the target attribute. At generation time, the model applies the editing process repeatedly, using a sequence of smaller changes to pursue a value beyond the observed range.

The authors evaluate ICE on a natural-language sentiment task and two protein-engineering tasks involving ACE2 stability and AAV fitness. They report that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in these evaluations despite its simplicity. The results support iterative refinement as a useful strategy for extrapolative generation: examples of modest improvements can train an editing process that is then applied repeatedly toward more ambitious targets.
icml-2023-extrapolative-controlled-seque.tldr: ICE learns small sequence improvements and applies them repeatedly to generate outputs with attribute values beyond the training range.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires retaining information from the forward computation for use during backpropagation. Pointwise activation functions appear throughout modern architectures, and the information stored for these operations contributes to memory consumption. This paper targets that cost by representing the activation-gradient information needed for the backward pass using only a few bits per element.

The authors formulate the task as finding an optimal piecewise-constant approximation to an activation function's derivative. Instead of retaining a high-precision derivative value, the method can represent it using one of a small number of values. Dynamic programming computes the optimal approximation, providing a systematic procedure for choosing the quantization.

The resulting activation operations are implemented as drop-in replacements for popular nonlinearities, allowing them to be incorporated into existing training pipelines. On several open benchmarks, the authors confirm reduced memory use with the same observed convergence. The findings indicate that substantial savings are possible in this particular part of the training memory footprint while preserving the tested models' learning behavior.
icml-2023-few-bit-backward-quantized-gra.tldr: Few-bit Backward reduces training memory by optimally quantizing activation derivatives, with unchanged convergence on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Language models can be expensive to run, creating demand for compression methods that reduce computation and inference latency. Existing pruning and distillation approaches may require labeled examples or time-consuming retraining to recover accuracy. This paper proposes a structured pruning framework that operates without gradients and uses only pretrained model weights and unlabeled data.

The approach aims to make compression practical when labeled downstream data is unavailable and the time available for adapting a model is limited. Its required inputs are the existing model and unlabeled examples, so the pruning procedure does not depend on obtaining task annotations. The reported process takes only a few minutes on a single GPU.

The authors evaluate BERT_BASE and DistilBERT on GLUE and SQuAD. Across the tasks considered, they report reductions of up to 40% in the original floating-point operation count with less than 4% accuracy loss. These findings demonstrate a favorable computation–accuracy tradeoff in the tested settings. The reported savings concern operation counts; the abstract does not claim an identical percentage reduction in inference latency.
icml-2023-gradient-free-structured-pruni.tldr: Gradient-free pruning uses pretrained weights and unlabeled data to reduce tested language models' FLOPs by up to 40% with less than 4% accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Adversarial accuracy is an important measure of whether a model withstands attacks, but it does not describe how many successful perturbations surround an input. Two models can therefore differ in aspects of robustness that this measure misses. This paper introduces adversarial sparsity to examine how difficult it is to find a successful perturbation when its direction is constrained.

The authors use this perspective to reveal differences among leading robust models that accuracy-based analysis does not capture. It also distinguishes defenses that are entirely ineffective from those that retain partial effectiveness despite failing against stronger attacks. This gives a more detailed account of what a defense accomplishes than a single accuracy result.

The paper further shows that robustness can improve under the sparsity measure without changing adversarial accuracy. In particular, data augmentation alone can produce such an improvement without adversarial training. The contribution is an additional evaluation perspective that exposes changes in vulnerability and can suggest ways to improve robustness, while retaining adversarial accuracy as an essential measure.
icml-2023-how-many-perturbations-break-t.tldr: Adversarial sparsity reveals differences in model vulnerability and defense effectiveness that adversarial accuracy alone can miss.

paragraphs: Training a classifier to resist adversarial attacks requires substantially more examples than ordinary classification. Diffusion models can supply useful synthetic images, but generating them is relatively slow. This paper examines how to make synthetic data more useful for robust learning, addressing the value of the generated examples alongside the broader concern about generation cost.

The authors first analyze the conditions a synthetic-data distribution should satisfy to improve robust accuracy. Their analysis identifies distinguishability among generated examples as critical. They then propose Contrastive-DP, which incorporates a contrastive loss into the diffusion generation process to guide the model toward data with this desirable property.

Simulations support the theoretical findings, and image-dataset experiments demonstrate good performance for the proposed method. The contribution links a property of the synthetic distribution to the downstream objective of adversarial robustness. It motivates steering generation according to what robust classification needs, so that the usefulness of synthetic training data becomes an explicit part of the generation procedure.
icml-2023-improving-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Contrastive-DP guides diffusion generation toward more distinguishable synthetic data to improve its usefulness for adversarially robust classification.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through a long sequence of denoising steps. Beyond making generation costly, this sequence can allow prediction errors to accumulate. The paper connects that behavior to exposure bias: training conditions on ground-truth samples, while generation must proceed using the model's own earlier results, which may already contain errors.

The proposed remedy is a simple training regularizer that perturbs the ground-truth samples used as inputs. These perturbations simulate the kinds of prediction errors encountered during generation. Training therefore exposes the model to imperfect inputs resembling those it will need to handle when its own outputs feed subsequent steps.

In the reported experiments, input perturbation improves sample quality while reducing both training and inference time, without affecting precision or recall. On CelebA at 64×64 resolution, the authors report an FID score of 1.27 and a 37.5% saving in training time. These results suggest that addressing the mismatch between training inputs and generated intermediate results can improve both quality and efficiency in the evaluated diffusion models.
icml-2023-input-perturbation-reduces-exp.tldr: Perturbing diffusion training inputs simulates generation errors, improving reported sample quality while reducing training and inference time.

paragraphs: A neural differential equation learns a dynamical system, but its computational cost depends on how many steps an adaptive numerical solver needs to follow that system. Earlier approaches to reducing this cost can increase training time or depend on particular training algorithms. This paper seeks dynamics that are easier to integrate while retaining flexibility in how gradients are computed.

The method uses cost heuristics already available inside adaptive solvers and evaluates them at randomly sampled times during training. These local signals guide the learned system toward behavior that the solver can handle more efficiently. The construction supports any sensitivity method, and the authors develop two sampling strategies that offer different tradeoffs between performance and training time.

Experiments report performance comparable to global regularization while preserving implementation flexibility. The number of function evaluations falls to between 0.556 and 0.733 times the comparison level, and predictions become 1.3 to 2 times faster. The results show that solver-aware training signals can reduce prediction cost without requiring the method to be tied to a particular gradient-computation approach.
icml-2023-locally-regularized-neural-dif.tldr: Local solver-cost regularization learns neural differential equations that are easier to integrate, accelerating predictions while supporting any sensitivity method.

paragraphs: Code-model benchmarks often cover only a narrow selection of programming languages. This paper introduces BabelCode, a framework for execution-based evaluation across benchmarks and languages, with visibility into memory use, runtime, and individual test outcomes. It also presents TP3, a translation dataset built around converting expert-level Python programming puzzles into other languages.

Using these tools, the authors investigate whether balancing a training corpus across 14 languages improves performance on languages with less training data. The balanced model achieves an average 12.34% improvement in pass@k across the evaluated tasks and languages relative to the baseline. This aggregate improvement comes with a redistribution of performance between language groups.

For low-resource languages, the reported pass@k improvement is 66.48%, accompanied by a 12.94% decrease for high-resource languages. Across three translation tasks, the corresponding averages are a 30.77% improvement and a 19.58% decrease. These findings make the training-distribution tradeoff concrete: broader support can benefit less represented languages substantially, while reducing performance on better represented ones in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-measuring-the-impact-of-progra.tldr: BabelCode and TP3 enable broader code-model evaluation, revealing that balanced language training improves low-resource performance with high-resource tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Prompt-tuning adapts a language model by learning a soft prompt from data. This paper studies how attention makes that adaptation effective using a simplified one-layer architecture. Its contextual data model separates input tokens into those relevant to the current context and those that are irrelevant, allowing the role of the learned prompt to be isolated.

Within this model, the authors prove that softmax prompt-attention is more expressive than both softmax self-attention and linear prompt-attention. They also analyze the early trajectory of gradient descent, showing near-optimal sample complexity for learning the prompt and prediction head. The analysis explains how a prompt can focus attention on relevant tokens even when those tokens are sparse.

A separate result characterizes exact finite-sample performance when the prompt is known but the prediction head is unknown. This identifies performance limits and quantifies the benefit of context information under that assumption. Experiments on real datasets support the theoretical insights. Together, the results give a conditional, mathematically explicit explanation of how prompt-tuning can select task-relevant information.
icml-2023-on-the-role-of-attention-in-pr.tldr: A one-layer contextual model explains how learned prompts improve expressiveness and direct attention toward sparse, relevant tokens.

paragraphs: Screening systems use predicted probabilities to decide which candidates enter a shortlist. A calibrated classifier supports a useful efficiency result: thresholding can identify the smallest shortlist containing a desired number of qualified candidates in expectation. This paper asks whether that justification is sufficient when considering how qualified people within the same demographic group are treated.

The authors argue that calibrated screening policies can still exhibit within-group unfairness. They identify within-group monotonicity as a property that can prevent this problem. This adds a requirement on how predictions behave within each group, addressing a concern that calibration alone does not resolve.

To make the requirement practical, the paper introduces an efficient dynamic-programming algorithm that post-processes a calibrated classifier. It minimally modifies the classifier so its probability estimates satisfy within-group monotonicity. Experiments using US Census survey data show that this property can often be achieved with a small cost in prediction granularity and shortlist size. The findings establish a concrete way to improve within-group treatment while measuring the resulting screening tradeoffs.
icml-2023-on-the-within-group-fairness-o.tldr: Within-group monotonicity addresses screening unfairness that calibration can miss, and a post-processing algorithm often achieves it at modest cost.

paragraphs: Entropic fictitious play optimizes an objective defined over probability measures, combining a convex functional with an entropy term. Such objectives arise when studying two-layer neural networks in the mean-field regime. This paper examines the algorithm when the learning objective has a finite-sum structure, connecting its theoretical behavior to a more practical implementation.

The authors develop a primal-dual analysis using properties of a proximal Gibbs measure. They establish quantitative global convergence guarantees for both continuous-time dynamics and discrete updates. Covering both formulations connects an idealized evolution of the algorithm with the step-by-step process used in computation, within the finite-sum setting they analyze.

The same framework yields a memory-efficient implementation that represents the measure using particles. It also suggests a relationship with gradient boosting, connecting this optimization approach to another family of learning methods. Experiments involving neural-network optimization and image synthesis illustrate the implementation's efficiency. The contribution combines convergence analysis and an implementation strategy, showing how the mathematical formulation can inform the resources needed to run the algorithm.
icml-2023-primal-and-dual-analysis-of-en.tldr: A primal-dual analysis gives entropic fictitious play global convergence guarantees and a memory-efficient particle implementation for finite-sum problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how pairwise augmentation affects the amount of data needed to learn an optimal decision boundary in binary linear classification. For a particular family of distributions, it compares the classifier minimizing training loss with the classifier achieving the best test accuracy. A separability parameter controls how distinctly the two classes are distributed.

The authors find that, without augmentation, increasing separability makes the sample requirement grow exponentially in that parameter. Thus, in this setting, more separable data can make identifying the optimal boundary harder. They prove that Mixup substantially reduces this sample complexity, mitigating what they call the curse of separability.

The analysis requires new concentration results because the many augmented pairs constructed from a dataset share original examples and are therefore dependent. The paper also examines masking-based Mixup variants and shows that they can distort the training objective, causing its minimizer to approach a classifier with suboptimal test accuracy. These results establish a benefit for Mixup in the analyzed setting while showing that related augmentation procedures need not preserve that benefit.
icml-2023-provable-benefit-of-mixup-for-.tldr: For a studied binary linear classification family, Mixup reduces the sample burden of finding optimal boundaries as class separability increases.

paragraphs: Image restoration reconstructs an image from degraded observations, which can correspond to multiple possible originals. Stochastic methods can explore these alternatives. This paper investigates additional advantages of randomness, focusing on whether restored outputs look perceptually correct, remain consistent with the observations, and withstand adversarial changes to the input.

The central theorem states that a restoration algorithm achieving both perfect perceptual quality and input consistency must sample from the posterior distribution. Under these requirements, stochastic behavior is necessary. The authors also illustrate how deterministic restoration can achieve high perceptual quality through an extremely sensitive mapping, leaving it vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

Their robustness results reveal a practical contrast: enforcing robustness strongly harms the perceptual quality of deterministic models, whereas robustifying stochastic models barely affects perceptual quality and improves output variability. The findings give a reason to pursue stochastic restoration beyond its ability to produce multiple answers. Randomness can help reconcile the competing demands of believable outputs, agreement with the degraded input, and resistance to perturbations.
icml-2023-reasons-for-the-superiority-of.tldr: The paper establishes conditional necessity for stochastic restoration and shows advantages in balancing perceptual quality, consistency, and robustness.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks offer efficient inference on long sequences but can be difficult to optimize and slow to train. Deep state-space models combine strong long-sequence performance with parallelizable training, raising the question of which design choices explain their advantage. This paper investigates whether carefully constructed recurrent networks can recover those benefits.

The authors analyze and ablate several changes to standard recurrent networks: making the recurrence linear and diagonal, improving parameterization and initialization, and carefully normalizing the forward computation. Their design is guided by arguments about how signals propagate through a network. The resulting recurrent block is called the Linear Recurrent Unit, or LRU.

On the Long Range Arena benchmark, LRU matches the reported performance and computational efficiency of deep state-space models. The study also shows that its carefully designed recurrent networks can match their training speed on long-range reasoning tasks. These findings help explain the source of state-space models' success by identifying recurrent design choices that recover comparable behavior in the evaluated setting.
icml-2023-resurrecting-recurrent-neural-.tldr: The Linear Recurrent Unit uses carefully designed linear recurrence to match deep state-space models' Long Range Arena performance and efficiency.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a good decision-making policy from previously collected data, without additional environment interaction. Large state-action spaces make both data coverage and function approximation important. Linear-programming formulations have offered a promising route, supporting sample-efficient learning under partial coverage and assumptions that the chosen function classes can represent the needed quantities.

This paper introduces a new formulation that relaxes certain assumptions in earlier results and achieves optimal statistical rates as a function of sample size. Its central design change is to impose suitable constraints in the optimization problem. Careful choices of function classes and initial-state distributions are also essential parts of the construction.

The authors use these constraints in place of the regularization employed in prior formulations. The resulting perspective clarifies how the structure of the optimization problem can improve statistical guarantees for offline learning. The contribution is theoretical: it advances the linear-programming framework and its associated primal-dual minimax optimization while retaining explicit attention to the assumptions needed for learning from limited existing data.
icml-2023-revisiting-the-linear-programm.tldr: A constrained linear-programming formulation relaxes some offline RL assumptions and achieves optimal statistical rates in sample size.

paragraphs: Sliced-Wasserstein distance offers a computationally efficient way to compare distributions by averaging comparisons over slices. Much less is understood about generalization when those slices are drawn from a distribution other than the usual uniform choice. This becomes particularly relevant when the distribution of slices is selected using the available data.

The paper observes that the sliced distance can be interpreted as an average risk, making it suitable for PAC-Bayesian analysis. The authors derive generalization bounds for adaptive Sliced-Wasserstein distances defined using arbitrary slice distributions, including data-dependent ones. These bounds provide a theoretical way to study how an adaptively chosen comparison relates to behavior beyond the observed samples.

The theory also leads to a procedure for learning the slice distribution by optimizing the bounds, with the goal of making the resulting distance maximally discriminative. Empirical illustrations support the theoretical findings. The contribution connects flexibility in selecting slices with a principled learning objective and generalization analysis, giving adaptive distribution comparisons a clearer statistical foundation.
icml-2023-shedding-a-pac-bayesian-light-.tldr: PAC-Bayesian bounds provide a statistical foundation and learning procedure for data-adaptive Sliced-Wasserstein distances.

paragraphs: A neural network with sparse weights contains many zero-valued connections, but realizing a training-speed benefit requires an implementation that can exploit that structure. SparseProp provides a specialized implementation of backpropagation for sparse networks. Its focus is making sparsity useful for the computations performed during training on ordinary CPU hardware.

The method supports arbitrary, unstructured sparsity, so it does not require nonzero weights to follow a particular regular arrangement. It also applies to common layer types, including convolutional and linear layers. The authors provide a fast vectorized CPU implementation, connecting the general sparse-backpropagation algorithm to execution on widely available processors.

End-to-end runtime experiments show that the implementation can accelerate transfer learning with networks that have already been sparsified, as well as training sparse networks from scratch. These two settings demonstrate usefulness across different starting points for model training. The paper presents its findings as the first support for sparse training on commodity hardware, with the reported speedups establishing that sparse computation can translate into improvements in complete training runs.
icml-2023-sparseprop-efficient-sparse-ba.tldr: SparseProp exploits unstructured weight sparsity to accelerate end-to-end neural-network training on commodity CPUs.

paragraphs: Multicalibration seeks predictions that satisfy calibration requirements across multiple groups. This paper asks which statistical properties can support that goal. It connects the answer to property elicitation: whether a target property can be characterized through an appropriate prediction loss. Under mild technical conditions, a continuous scalar property admits multicalibrated prediction exactly when it is elicitable.

The negative result is strong: for non-elicitable continuous properties, simple distributions exist where even the true distributional predictor fails calibration. On the positive side, the authors give canonical learning algorithms for elicitable properties in both batch and online adversarial settings. These results generalize work on means and quantiles and strengthen earlier online quantile guarantees.

The paper also identifies a route around some individual-property impossibilities. If one property becomes elicitable conditional on another elicitable property, an algorithm can jointly multicalibrate the pair. This extends earlier mean-moment results. Applications to fair risk assessment yield both new algorithms and impossibility results, clarifying which calibration objectives are achievable directly and which require a richer joint prediction target.
icml-2023-the-statistical-scope-of-multi.tldr: Under mild conditions, elicitation characterizes which continuous scalar properties admit multicalibration, with joint prediction enabling additional cases.

paragraphs: Privileged information consists of features available during training that will not be available when a model is used. Such information can help learning from noisy labels, but the reasons are not obvious. This paper investigates which properties make these extra training features useful through experiments with real privileged information and a new large-scale benchmark, ImageNet-PI.

Across the studied datasets, privileged information is most helpful when it makes clean and noisy examples easy to distinguish while providing a shortcut for memorizing the noisy examples. The experiments also reveal a counterintuitive pattern: when privileged information becomes too predictive of the target label, methods using it often perform worse than corresponding methods without it.

These findings guide enhancements to existing leading privileged-information methods. The authors also show that the resulting approaches can be combined with established label-noise methods that do not use privileged information. The contribution clarifies that the usefulness of extra training features depends on what they reveal about noise and how the model uses them, rather than simply how strongly they predict the label.
icml-2023-when-does-privileged-informati.tldr: Privileged information helps noisy-label learning most when it separates clean from noisy examples and enables memorization of the noisy ones.
